li.a: Los Angeles Times, 21 June 1985: Massacre That 'Woke Everybody Up' Helped Bring Truce in Sri Lanka
Time, 27 May 1985: Sri Lanka Tamil Terror
Colombo Telegraph: The Paul Nallanayagam Case and the Anuradhapura Massacre
Hiru News (Gold FM): The LTTE attack on Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi marks 28 years
Daily Mirror, 20 February 2025: Disturbing Activities that Threaten Wilpattu National Park
Borealis Threat and Risk: 146 Buddhist pilgrims killed in the Anuradhapura massacre (May 14, 1985)

content.p: On 14 May 1985 a group of Tamil guerrillas from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam attacked Anuradhapura, a city in north-central Sri Lanka largely inhabited by Buddhist Sinhalese. They opened fire on crowds at the main bus station, then drove to the Sri Maha Bodhi shrine, where worshippers were gathered around a bo tree believed to descend from the one under which the Buddha attained awakening. The Los Angeles Times called it the most terrifying episode in the decade-long Tamil separatist conflict and reported that 146 civilians, most of them Buddhist Sinhalese, were killed.

The death toll is still given in more than one form. The accounts agree on the outline of the day and on the 146 figure in most cases, but they differ on how many died, how many buses were used, and whether the attackers went on to a national park afterwards.
content.h2: Land mines and the Valvettithurai killings
content.p: The violence that preceded the attack was already part of a rising pattern. According to Colombo Telegraph, two land mine attacks by the LTTE on 7 and 9 May 1985 at Valvettithurai, the hometown of the LTTE leader, killed ten soldiers and an army major. Citing a Saturday Review report, the article says the Army surrounded the town on 10 May, took 24 young men to the community centre and blew it up. It adds that 12 civilians were killed at the Theertha Madam, a resting place beside the temple's sacred tank, and 34 more in other parts of the town, bringing the toll to 70. The Los Angeles Times reported the same 70 deaths and attributed them to government troops.

The wider context was a political shift in India. Indira Gandhi had been assassinated in October 1984 and her son Rajiv became prime minister. The Los Angeles Times reported that Rajiv Gandhi declared at a press conference, "We will not allow Eelam," ruling out a separate Tamil state. Colombo Telegraph writes that by the spring of 1985 there were signs India was exerting greater control over the Tamil militant groups and moving towards a ceasefire.

Time magazine, reporting a week later, described the first stage this way: separatist guerrillas from the mostly Hindu Tamil minority seized a bus and set off for Anuradhapura, where most residents are Buddhist Sinhalese. As they drove into the crowded main bus station they opened fire with automatic weapons, killing, in Time's estimate, about 100 men, women and children.

The accounts differ on how the attackers arrived. Borealis Threat and Risk, a consultancy blog written by a former official of Canada's intelligence service, says the group hijacked a bus, got off it and sprayed crowds of worshippers with gunfire. Hiru News says the LTTE "snatched a public bus" and stormed the central bus stand in the old town. Colombo Telegraph, quoting the official document, says dozens of LTTE men in military uniform arrived in two buses and began firing on civilians.

From the bus station, Time reports, the group went to the Sri Maha Bodhiya, the sacred site of the bo tree, and fired into a crowd that included nuns and monks. Time put the bo tree at about 2,200 years old; the Los Angeles Times gave 2,500 years. Time describes the crowd there as including nuns and monks.

Time says the attackers then continued towards the north-west coast, attacking a police station and a game reserve on the way, and may have escaped by boat to India. Colombo Telegraph gives a different route: the attackers escaped along the Puttalam Road into the Wilpattu wildlife area without a single shot being fired at them.

The Daily Mirror, writing in February 2025 about threats to Wilpattu National Park, says that on 14 May 1985 terrorists killed 24 wildlife officers at the park's headquarters, the largest number of wildlife officers to die at a single location. The same article says that 36 wildlife officers have died in the service of Wilpattu in total. The 1985 reports used here give no figure for Wilpattu, so the 24 is the Daily Mirror's claim.

The figure most often repeated for Anuradhapura is 146. The Los Angeles Times reported that 146 civilians were killed, most of them Buddhist Sinhalese. Time gave the same total for the whole bus station and shrine attack. Hiru News and Borealis Threat and Risk both describe 146 pilgrims killed, with 85 wounded.

Colombo Telegraph gives a lower figure. It quotes an official document titled "Massacre of Civilians" which put the number of Sinhalese civilians killed at 120, including pilgrims at the Great Bo Tree premises, with 85 injured. The article does not say why the figures differ, and the other accounts do not settle which is right. A reader should therefore treat 146 as the figure most of these accounts use, and 120 as the figure in the official document as quoted by Colombo Telegraph.

Time wrote that the killings that week, by its count, amounted to the slaughter of more than 200 people, and that the bus ride through Anuradhapura, the shrine and the north-west coast "resulted in the massacre of 146 people."

The Los Angeles Times reported that the LTTE took responsibility for the massacre and said it was revenge for the killing of 70 Tamil civilians by government troops at Valvettithurai the week before. Colombo Telegraph also gives 70 dead at Valvettithurai in the days before the attack.

The LTTE's stated reason is not the only account. Colombo Telegraph notes that later reports in the international media said India's intelligence agency had asked other Tamil militant groups to carry out such an attack and that they had refused. The article presents this as a report rather than an established fact, and asks whether any attack of this kind could have been carried out without Indian clearance "needs to be questioned." Hiru News, in an anniversary report, took the view that the attack was planned by the LTTE leader himself, to inflame communal hatred and provoke mob attacks on Tamil civilians across the island. That report gives no evidence for the claim on the page.

Time wrote that the guerrillas, by attacking a sacred Buddhist site, "seemed almost eager to provoke retaliation." It said retaliation came quickly. Off the northern coast near Jaffna, Time reported, 39 Tamil passengers were cut down with blades after a group boarded a ferry. The Sri Lankan navy denied that it was involved. The same day, Time said, police killed 20 Tamil fighters who had been sheltering in a cave in the Eastern Province.

The Los Angeles Times reported that more Tamil civilians were killed after Anuradhapura. Among them were nine people who had gone to an army camp seeking refuge and were shot by an army corporal, who kept firing until his commanding officer shot him.

Time reported that at the end of the week the president, J. R. Jayewardene, who was also defence minister and commander of the armed forces, had not visited the site of the massacre. Public anger grew over the government's apparent paralysis, Time said.

In June 1985 a ceasefire was announced between government forces and the main Tamil separatist groups. The Los Angeles Times reported, on the basis of interviews with government officials, politicians and academics, that public shock over the massacre had done more than any other factor to bring it about. A senior Asian diplomat was quoted saying, "The Anuradhapura incident woke everybody up." The Sinhalese sociologist Reggie Siriwardena told the paper: "Public opinion has shifted. I think, in fact, it was Anuradhapura that changed the situation." He also said the attack "brought home the war to the Sinhala people," and that "it was horrible and indefensible, I agree."

The Los Angeles Times reported that the attack pushed the government to ask India for help and opened the way for a political settlement. A senior official told the paper that, for the first time, the government would seriously consider some degree of regional autonomy for the Tamil areas of the north and east. The Tamil United Liberation Front spokesman, Apapillai Amirthalingam, said in Madras that the militants had agreed to the ceasefire "in deference to Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi's wishes," as Reuters reported.

Several details are not settled by the sources. The death toll is given as 146 by most of the sources and as 120 by the official document quoted by Colombo Telegraph. The number of buses is given as one by Time and Borealis, and as two by Colombo Telegraph. Time estimated about 100 deaths at the bus station, but gave no breakdown for the shrine. The age of the bo tree is given as 2,200 years by Time and 2,500 by the Los Angeles Times. The wildlife officer toll at Wilpattu is given as 24 by the Daily Mirror in 2025, and the 1985 reports do not give one.

What the sources agree on is that on 14 May 1985 guerrillas attacked civilians in a sacred Buddhist city, and that the attack killed at least 120 people. The Los Angeles Times reported the LTTE's claim that it was revenge, and that the attack was followed by more killings of Tamil civilians and by a change in the government's approach to the conflict.
